Consider the other two major, legal, recreational drugs in America: alcohol and tobacco.

Consider the damage to public health and safety caused by these, and importantly, that the damage is not limited to just the user.

Legislated prohibition of alcohol, at a time when it was already culturally ingrained (1920s), failed and was repealed. Alcohol and its public health and safety ills are here to stay. Millions of dollars will continue to be spent each year on prevention and treatment of these ills.

Legislative prohibition of tobacco, after it had become culturally ingrained, never got off the ground (at the federal level). Tobacco and its public health and safety ills are here to stay. Millions of dollars will continue to be spent each year on prevention and treatment of these ills.

I have seen nothing convincing in studies of the drug, or human nature, that suggest anything different will happen with marijuana. How many years will pass before we discover the consequences that were not immediately apparent (as when people realized cigarette smoking was unhealthy)? At that point, being culturally ingrained and therefore impossible to legislate away, how many more years will we spend millions upon millions on prevention and treatment?

Decades of effort and money from groups both private and governmental have led to a shift in attitudes about tobacco use, which has led to some states and municipalities choosing to legislate varying degrees of tobacco prohibition. The notion of tobacco use is slowly becoming less-widely culturally ingrained, and with that shift comes the success of legislative prohibition. We have witnessed the rise, and I believe we are now witnessing the fall, of the use of this drug in the United States - and with it, its public health menace. Have we not learned our lesson, and now wish to repeat this with a new drug?

That is why I do not support legalization of recreational marijuana use.

Notes:

  1. I support decriminalization of all drugs. Portugal's approach significantly reduced the public health ills caused by drug abuse and I think there is something worthwhile to be found there.

  2. I fully support investigating the medical applications of marijuana and compounds derived from the plant. researchers should absolutely be able to work with it and fold any useful discoveries into our normal medical practice. Morphine, a drug that is not ( and in my opinion should not be ) in widespread recreational use, is nonetheless very useful when properly administered by a medical professional.

  3. At an individual level, I support the legalization of all drugs. People should be able to do whatever they want to their own bodies, as long as they do it responsibly and do not endanger or burden those around them. From a public-policy point of view however, this is never the way it shakes out (law of large numbers), and therefore I could never support carte blanche legalization of all drugs.

  4. Decriminalize, work to reduce and minimize the harms caused by use and abuse, and begin seriously evaluating its effects - both in medical and recreational contexts. If a meaningfully-large body of hard science (widely studied and repeated by researchers not in fear of federal law) turns out that recreational use has a minimal impact on public health and safety, then is the time to consider legalization. Not before. Not now.

There is the issue that to date, as far as I know, there is no reliable road side test for marijuana use (or more specifically recent marijuana use indicating impairment). We have a big enough problem with people driving under the influence of alcohol that to add another mind/reaction impairing drug to the mix doesn't exactly help the issue.

Then there's the act of smoking itself. Admittedly people don't chain smoke joints quite the same way as cigarettes but at the end of the day you are still inhaling smoke into your lungs which can't be good.
It's not that I'm against legalization, it's just that it makes people stupid and easily manipulated when used regularly.

Playing Devil's Advocate here.

You have to draw a line somewhere with public health issues. You can't ban everything that has a negative impact on the body, but it's equally ludicrous to allow everything. If for no other reason than to keep our already-strained healthcare resources from having to deal with the influx of overdoses and accidents due to widened "drug" use.

Debate the appropriateness of the line between alcohol and marijuana, but the fact of the matter is that it's a reasonable enough place to put the line. Could it be better? Probably. But what purpose does it serve to continue debating whether or not that line should be moved? In other words, instead of asking "What harm is it", ask "What benefit is it".
